subtopic: Using AI tools for learning without cheating
subtype: Approach: correcting course after crossing the line [Revision]
passage: I'm Aditi, and I'll be honest: I submitted a history assignment that was about ninety percent AI. I told myself I'd rewrite it later. I didn't. Three days later the class was discussing my topic and I couldn't say a word, and I felt sick, not because I might get caught, but because it wasn't mine. That evening I decided to tell Yusuf Sir before anyone asked. I walked to the staffroom with cold hands and said it straight. He was quiet, then said, “Thank you for telling me, beti.” I would lose the marks for that submission and had to redo it. I said, “I know.” I rewrote it that week in my own words, slowly and badly at first. And I made a rule: AI can explain, never write. The mark was lower. But I can talk about that topic now.

qa.q: What did Aditi decide to do that evening?
qa.a: Aditi decided to tell Yusuf Sir before anyone asked.

qa.q: What was Aditi feeling when she could not say a word in class?
qa.a: Aditi felt sick with guilt, since the work was not hers.

qa.q: Which choice worked in Aditi's story, and why?
qa.a: Telling the teacher and redoing the work in her own words worked, because it fixed the problem and the learning finally happened.

qa.q: How might Yusuf Sir see Aditi's confession?
qa.a: Yusuf Sir probably appreciates her honesty, since he thanks her, even as he applies the consequence.

grounding: A teen who submitted mostly AI-written work realises it was wrong, tells the teacher, redoes it in her own words and sets a rule, accepting a consequence.

subtopic: Using AI tools for learning without cheating
subtype: Approach: correcting course after crossing the line [Revision]
passage: I share a bench with Gopika, so I saw most of it. Last Monday she was quiet all through maths. At lunch she told me she'd submitted the science project on renewable energy mostly written by an AI tool, and she couldn't stop thinking about it. "It's got my name on it and it isn't mine," she said. After lunch she went to Mr. Varghese. I waited outside the staffroom. When she came out, her eyes were red, but she looked steadier. She told me he'd given her a week to redo it, written by her this time, and the marks would be capped at half. Every evening that week she wrote in the library, and I saw a new line on the first page of her notebook: "AI: ideas and checking only. Never the writing." I'm Maria, by the way. I'm not sure I'd have been that brave.

qa.q: What was the science project about?
Why did Gopika go to Mr. Varghese?
qa.a: Gopika felt guilty and uncomfortable that work with her name on it wasn't hers, and couldn't stop thinking about it.

qa.q: What else could Gopika do to keep her new rule?
qa.a: She could tell Mr. Varghese about the rule and note how AI was used on each assignment, so it stays visible.

qa.q: How does Maria see what Gopika did?
qa.a: Maria admires it as brave and isn't sure of being able to own up in the same way.

grounding: Shows a teen who submitted mostly AI-written work telling the teacher, redoing it in her own words with capped marks, and setting a rule for future use.

subtopic: Using AI tools for learning without cheating
subtype: Approach: correcting course after crossing the line [Revision]
passage:
Friday. Keerthana clicked submit on the English essay at 11:58 pm. Most of it had come from an AI tool; she had changed only a few words. She lay awake, thinking of the line in the class rules: work must be your own.
Monday. Before first period, she stood at Chetan Sir's desk. "Sir, my essay isn't really mine. Most of it was written by AI. I'm sorry." He was quiet, then said, "I appreciate you telling me. You'll rewrite it by Thursday. The mark will be out of fifteen, not twenty." Keerthana nodded. "That's fair."
Two weeks later. For the next essay, Keerthana wrote the whole draft herself first, then asked the tool only to point out grammar mistakes. A sticky note on her laptop read: "My words first. Always." She got sixteen out of twenty, and it felt better than any borrowed twenty.

qa.q: What time did Keerthana submit the essay?
Why did Keerthana lie awake on Friday night?
qa.a: Keerthana felt guilty, thinking of the class rule that work must be your own.

qa.q: What else could Keerthana do if tempted again near a deadline?
qa.a: She could start drafting earlier or ask Chetan Sir for more time, rather than letting a tool write it.

qa.q: How might Chetan Sir see Keerthana's confession?
qa.a: He values the honesty, thanking her, but still gives a fair consequence, which keeps the rule meaningful for the class.

grounding: Illustrates a teen owning up to an AI-written essay, accepting a lower cap, rewriting it and setting a rule for later work.
